title: Holocare
summary: Speculative AI app that scans minor injuries and guides treatment. WCAG-audited and tested over two rounds.

hero.alt: Several phones laid out at an angle showing Holocare screens: the login, an injury scan, a chat about a wound photo and a progress checklist.

sections.heading: At a Glance
body: Project: Holocare, a speculative AI-powered injury assessment app
Role: Product Designer, UX Researcher (team project)
Duration: 4 weeks (10–31 July 2024)
Tools: Figma, Premiere Pro

sections.heading: Introduction
body: Access to immediate, reliable healthcare information matters. My team and I designed an app that uses artificial intelligence to scan minor injuries and help treat them. The goal was a simple platform that guides people through assessment and treatment, so they get clear advice quickly.
The project was showcased at UNSW’s Design After Dark event.

sections.heading: Problem Statement
body: Minor injuries aren’t life-threatening, but uncertainty about how serious they are causes stress. Getting advice usually means a visit to a healthcare professional or a long online search.

In 2023, 1.9 million injuries ended up in emergency departments, and the home was the most common place of injury (AIHW, 2024). Our own primary research found that most people forget what a medical professional tells them, and 33% lack the knowledge to treat an injury properly. That is what led us to design the app, and to gamify aftercare so people stick with it.

media.alt: Slide titled “Context and Problems”: 1,900,000 injuries ended up in emergency departments in 2023, and 162,000 cases happened at home.
media.caption: Context from AIHW data.

sections.heading: Objective and Target Users
body: We set out to design a mobile app that uses AI to scan and assess minor injuries and offers personalised treatment advice. It needed to be intuitive, accessible and trustworthy, so people could confidently manage minor injuries at home.
Our audience is adults aged 18 and over with little or no knowledge of treatment and aftercare. It also helps people in remote areas or with limited access to medical care.

sections.heading: 1. Ideation
body: We started with brainstorming, sketching features and user flows. The focus was a short path from scanning an injury to receiving treatment advice. This led to our first prototype sketches and a storyboard for the showcase video.

media.alt: Hand-drawn storyboard in twelve panels: a person hurts their hand, scans it with the app, follows the advice and recovers.
media.caption: Storyboard for the showcase video.

sections.heading: 2. Wireframing and Accessibility
body: In Figma we built low-fidelity wireframes of the key screens: the injury scan, assessment results and treatment recommendations, keeping them simple enough for users of all ages.
We audited the design against WCAG 2.0, checking colour contrast, text scaling, keyboard navigation and screen reader support.

media.alt: Hand-drawn low-fidelity prototype of the app’s screens: login, home, scan, treatment, chat, history and aftercare.
media.caption: Low-fidelity prototype.

sections.heading: 3. Prototyping
body: We tested a medium-fidelity prototype with two tasks, then built a high-fidelity prototype in Figma using that feedback: a clean interface, clear navigation and step-by-step instructions.

media.alt: Figma canvas with the high-fidelity screens connected into flows: intro, home, injury scan, medicine list, chat, hospital and appointment booking.
media.caption: High-fidelity prototype in Figma.

sections.heading: 4. Second Iteration
body: Testing showed the app needed more visual appeal and more of the gamified aftercare we had planned. We added a personalised avatar that shows where you’re injured, so people who dislike seeing blood or wounds can still follow their injury, along with bigger text, clearer buttons and medication and pharmacy recommendations.

We tested again with three tasks: scan an injury and book an appointment, check a previous injury and finish its aftercare, and check the medicine you need. Every task took under a minute on average, and people rated the app 4 out of 5 for engagement.

Testers also asked to confirm what the AI had detected before acting on it. Keeping a person in the loop builds trust in an AI result, so it became a requirement for the next version, alongside a smoother flow.

media.alt: Annotated screens from the second iteration: an avatar on the home screen, bigger text, new buttons, the wound shown on the avatar and medication recommendations.
media.caption: Changes from feedback, including the avatar.

media.alt: Slide of second-iteration results: three tasks, each completed in under a minute; engagement 4 out of 5; users asked to confirm the AI detection and for a smoother flow.
media.caption: Second-round results and new requirements.

sections.heading: 5. Final Product
body: The final design is an accessible app that helps people assess and treat minor injuries with confidence. Key features:
– AI injury scan: take a photo of an injury and get an immediate assessment.
– Personalised treatment advice: treatment steps, plus when to seek professional help.
– Accessible design, audited against WCAG 2.0: high-contrast mode, scalable text and screen reader support.
– A clear interface that makes the next step obvious.
– Injury history: save assessments to look back on or share with a healthcare professional.

media.alt: Final app screens laid out in a grid, beside three photos of a hand being scanned through the app with an overlay.
media.caption: Final app walkthrough.

sections.heading: Impact and Reception
body: Holocare was featured at UNSW’s Design After Dark, where industry professionals and peers responded well to its use of AI in healthcare and its accessible, user-centred design.
It tackles a common pain point and shows how AI can make everyday healthcare more accessible, as long as the design keeps people informed and in control.
